item.title: TUM: legacy portal harvested central-login passwords, an admin's credentials reached TUMonline; MFA accounts held
item.description: The Technical University of Munich said on 2026-11-06 that unknown attackers attacked its myTUM portal and captured the central-login passwords of all persons who had signed in there, among them the credentials of a TUMonline system administrator, with which they attacked the campus-management system TUMonline, which TUM took off the network. TUM says accounts with multi-factor authentication were protected, reported the incident to the Bavarian data-protection commissioner and filed a criminal complaint; heise reports that the entry point was a legacy system and that about 60,000 users are concerned.
item.content:encoded:
ROUTINENATOA2

Technical University of Munich: attackers captured the central-login passwords of everyone who signed in to the legacy myTUM portal, took a TUMonline system administrator's credentials and attacked the campus-management system; accounts with MFA were protected

The Technical University of Munich says unknown persons attacked its myTUM portal and captured the passwords for the central login to TUM systems, among them login.tum.de and TUMonline, from all persons who had logged in to myTUM; among them were the access credentials of a system administrator for TUMonline, with which the attackers attacked the central campus-management system TUMonline, which TUM then took off the network (translated from German) (TUM, 2026-11-06). TUM says the attackers may have reached the account password, name, private address and date of birth of everyone affected, plus staff and student details, that the attackers' accesses within TUMonline were largely logged and that it currently assumes no further TUMonline data such as grades is affected, and that accounts with multi-factor authentication were protected in this attack (translated from German) (TUM, 2026-11-06). heise, quoting a TUM spokesperson, reports that the attackers entered through a legacy system and that whether data was exfiltrated is still being investigated, and adds that about 60,000 students and employees are concerned (translated from German) (heise online, 2026-11-06). Neither source states how the passwords were captured at myTUM.

Exposure
A public university or other public body that keeps a retired or secondary sign-in portal validating against its central directory, so that every password typed there is a credential for the primary identity and administration systems; TUM's accounts with MFA held, and the lesson transfers to Swiss cantonal and university portals.
Defender takeaway
Inventory legacy and secondary portals that accept the central directory password and retire them or put them behind MFA, require MFA on administrator accounts of campus and school-management systems, and check whether an administrator ever signed in to such a portal.

item.title: Aargau's information-security law and ordinance take effect 1 January 2027; a specialist unit is to get directive powers
item.description: The Aargau government council announced on 2026-11-06 that it adopted the information-security ordinance (InfoSiV) and that the information-security law (InfoSiG) and the ordinance enter into force on 1 January 2027. An information-security specialist unit is to advise cantonal bodies with directive and enforcement powers, and a cantonal cyber coordination office, headed from that date by Bernhard Droz, and a personnel-security-vetting unit sit at the cantonal police.
item.content:encoded:
ROUTINENATOA2

Canton Aargau adopts its information-security ordinance (InfoSiV) and sets 1 January 2027 for the information-security law and ordinance, with a specialist unit to receive directive and enforcement powers and a cyber coordination office at the cantonal police

The Aargau government council adopted the information-security ordinance (InfoSiV) and decided that the information-security legislation, the law (InfoSiG) and the ordinance, enters into force on 1 January 2027 (translated from German) (Kanton Aargau, 2026-11-06). The canton says the law anchors uniform standards and a holistic information-security system in the cantonal administration, that an information-security specialist unit is to advise the cantonal bodies and be equipped with directive and enforcement powers so that one detection and defence strategy can be implemented, and that a further specialist unit for personnel security vetting and a cantonal cyber coordination office are being set up, both at the cantonal police (translated from German) (Kanton Aargau, 2026-11-06). The government elected Bernhard Droz, currently head of IT forensics and cybercrime at the cantonal police, as head of the cyber coordination office from 1 January 2027 (translated from German) (Kanton Aargau, 2026-11-06).

The communiqué says nothing about communes or other bearers of public tasks. In February 2025 Netzwoche reported that a majority in the consultation approved bringing them into the law's scope and that entry into force was then planned for 1 July 2026, so the final text decides whether communal bodies are bound (Netzwoche, 2025-02-24).

Exposure
Aargau cantonal bodies from 1 January 2027; whether communes and other bearers of public tasks fall in scope is not stated in the communiqué.
Defender takeaway
From 1 January 2027 Aargau cantonal bodies answer to one information-security specialist unit that is to be equipped to issue binding directives, so the 2026 task is reading the ordinance and the directives the specialist unit issues; the canton describes the unit's planned powers and not detailed duties, and communal IT owners should read the final text to see whether they are covered.

item.title: Oneconsult: a site granted a folder in Chrome or Edge can steal tokens and plant VS Code and PowerShell persistence
item.description: Oneconsult's analysis of Chromium's Windows blocklist shows that a website granted a folder through the File System Access API after two clicks keeps a handle for as long as the tab is open, and that the blocklist leaves .vscode, .Azure, C:\Users\Public, SMB shares and, after a OneDrive Known Folder Move, the Desktop reachable. The paths it demonstrates are token and .env theft, a fake VS Code extension and PowerShell profile or module backdoors that need the Bypass or Unrestricted execution policy, and a file proxy through the open tab that EDR sees only as browser file activity.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

Oneconsult on the File System Access API: after two clicks a website holds read and write access to folders such as .vscode, .Azure, the public desktop and SMB shares in Chrome and Edge, enough for token theft and persistence without a process on the host

Oneconsult analyses, from the Chromium source and tests on Windows 11 with Chrome and Edge 150.0.7871.101, what a website can reach through the File System Access API once a user selects a folder and grants permission: the handle stays valid as long as the tab is open and is obtained after just two user clicks (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02). Chrome rejects blocklisted paths, but a path that is not in its table and not an ancestor of a blocked path is allowed, and the kDontBlockChildren rule leaves the subfolders of listed directories selectable; Oneconsult confirmed .vscode, the Azure token cache, C:\Users\Public and SMB shares as accessible (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02).

Oneconsult demonstrates these paths. A site can search a granted folder and take files such as cached Azure tokens and .env files. It can drop a fake VS Code extension into .vscode/extensions, which runs inside the normal code.exe process and is unaffected by Mark of the Web because Node.js does not check the Zone.Identifier stream. It can plant PowerShell profile and module backdoors, which work only with the Bypass or Unrestricted execution policy because the API stamps every written file with ZoneId=3 and RemoteSigned refuses such files. It can drop files on the public desktop, where they appear for all users and trigger a warning that a certain percentage of users acknowledge. And it can run an interactive file proxy through the still-open tab, where EDR sees only the browser reading and writing files (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02). A OneDrive Known Folder Move enabled while Chrome is running leaves a stale blocklist, so the redirected Desktop was writable; Oneconsult notes that the bypass has been reported to Google, which made the issue public, and that Google classed reading a single dragged file from a blocked folder as "not a security issue" (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02).

Daniel Oz's July write-up of the same technique has a website edit a file the user already holds. He says the user-gesture requirement does not prevent phishing, only automatic picker invocation, and that signed or complex files may fail, be blocked or break in a way that prevents execution (Oz, 2026-07-05).

Exposure
Windows users of Chrome or Edge, above all developer workstations with VS Code, cached Azure tokens or PowerShell on the Bypass or Unrestricted execution policy, and estates that enable OneDrive Known Folder Move; the attack needs a user to choose a folder and confirm a second prompt (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02).
Detection
File-write telemetry for PowerShell profile paths, PowerShell module folders and .vscode\extensions, and changes to the Zone.Identifier stream there, whose ReferrerUrl and HostUrl fields keep the origin of the page that wrote the file (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02). Oz says editing a file does not automatically reclassify it as downloaded, so the stream is a possible marker, not a guaranteed one (Oz, 2026-07-05).

Triage: browsers legitimately read and write files for web editors such as Google Docs and VS Code for Web, as Oneconsult notes; the signal is a browser process writing into a persistence location, not the file activity itself.

Defender takeaway
Restrict file system read and write access with the Chrome Enterprise policies Oneconsult names, FileSystemReadAskForUrls, FileSystemWriteAskForUrls and the respective AskForUrls policies, alert on writes to PowerShell profiles and VS Code extension folders, and treat a website's request to choose a local folder as a social-engineering step (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02).

item.title: Kaspersky: ESXi and Proxmox ransomware ran on a monitoring server's root password and admin notes, no VM escape
item.description: Kaspersky's Global Emergency Response Team describes two ransomware cases in virtualised estates. In the BlackNevas case a PRTG Network Monitor held ESXi root access and the same root password was reused across hosts, so the attacker connected over SSH, disabled the execInstalledOnly policy with esxcli, ran the encryptor and deleted logs; in the case attributed to The Gentlemen the actor found Proxmox root credentials in plaintext notes on an administrator workstation and used the VNC web socket to encrypt the cluster. Kaspersky stresses that no VM escape was needed.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

Kaspersky GERT: two ESXi and Proxmox ransomware cases in which a monitoring server's reused root password and plaintext administrator notes, not a VM escape, gave the attackers the hypervisor

In the first case, Kaspersky's investigation began with BlackNevas ransomware activity on a Windows system in a virtualised domain-controller segment, where the execution of the AnyDesk remote tool and the GMER binary was recorded (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06). The environment used PRTG Network Monitor, whose deployment had broad access to the ESXi hosts, and the same root password was reused across several nodes; after obtaining access to the monitoring environment the attacker used the ESXi credential to connect over SSH to the hosts that shared the password (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06). On the first host, a file was uploaded during a root SSH session and its first execution failed with "Execution of non-installed file prevented"; the actor then disabled the execInstalledOnly policy with esxcli and ran it, while on a second host in another subnet with the same password the binary ran and the logs were cleared (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06).

In the second case, a ransomware incident by The Gentlemen, the actor used information it had collected between initial access and visible impact: on a compromised system administrator's workstation it found Proxmox root credentials and access details in plain-text notes and logged in as root (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06). It then activated the VNC web socket through the root account, which gave it control of the Proxmox environment, and used that access to download and run the ransomware in the cluster, encrypting the whole virtual environment (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06). Kaspersky says a fully patched hypervisor can still be compromised through a shared password, an overprivileged monitoring account, an open SSH path or an administrator interface reachable from a general server network (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06).

Exposure
A virtualisation estate where a monitoring, backup or management server stores or can use hypervisor root credentials, where one root password is shared across hosts, where SSH to ESXi is reachable from general server networks, or where administrators keep Proxmox or ESXi credentials in plain-text notes; PRTG, which supports storing VMware credentials at device or group level, is the product Kaspersky names (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06).
Detection
On ESXi, root SSH logins from addresses that do not normally administer the hosts, a file upload followed by a failed execution of a non-installed file, a change to the execInstalledOnly setting and cleared logs; on Proxmox, root@pam requests to the VNC web socket used to reach other hosts, as the log records Kaspersky shows (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06). Kaspersky advises alerting when execInstalledOnly, Secure Boot enforcement, Lockdown Mode, SSH, local accounts or remote logging settings change (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06).
Defender takeaway
Give each monitoring platform its own least-privilege identity instead of ESXi root, replace stored root passwords with vault retrieval or limited tokens, administer ESXi through vCenter with Lockdown Mode and SSH stopped by default, and keep logs off the hosts so a compromised administrator cannot erase them (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06).

item.title: BOSSAI AI agents took emergency-services data through open ports, public APIs and default credentials
item.description: Acronis TRU describes BOSSAI, an agentic campaign it attributes with high confidence to one operator in Taiwan: a mesh of 12 AI agents, nine active, that over 12 observed days targeted government emergency services, banks, universities and military systems in 11 countries, with confirmed data exfiltration or system access at roughly ten targets in three countries. The confirmed emergency-services harm was patient-care records of a Taipei fire department and dispatch case records of a city 119 system; TRU says the agents failed where authentication was enforced and endpoints were filtered.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB3

Acronis TRU on BOSSAI: one operator's mesh of 12 AI agents took patient-care records and dispatch case data from Taiwanese emergency services through a legacy open port, a public API and default root credentials, and failed wherever authentication was enforced

Acronis TRU found an open attack workstation holding more than 90,000 files and describes BOSSAI as a mesh of 12 AI agents, nine active, driven by a changing roster of language models, with the operator acting as the bridge between agents and typing commands in Traditional Chinese (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04). The agents that executed attacks ran almost exclusively on abliterated open-weight models run locally, after commercial models repeatedly refused offensive requests (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04). In the 12 days TRU observed, the operator targeted government emergency services, banks and lenders, universities and military systems in 11 countries, with confirmed exfiltration or system access at roughly ten targets in three countries and about fifteen more attacked without confirmed compromise (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04).

The confirmed emergency-services harm is the part that matters here. A Taipei fire-department patient-care records platform exposed ECG readings, ambulance video and vital signs from 2018, accessible without credentials; a city's 119 dispatch system yielded case records with incident times, response types, status fields and street-level locations across seven districts from the system's API; and a fire-dispatch vendor's database administration panel opened with default root credentials, exposing 18 or more tables (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04). In an emergency-management system the agents found a hardcoded AES-256 key in front-end JavaScript that exposed session-cookie contents, an administrator identity among them, and a partial server-side request forgery path, without confirming a full compromise (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04). A brute-force run against a national fire agency's single sign-on portal gave no confirmed access, and the critical Apache flaw that the operator's vulnerability platform reported at a disaster-response centre was fabricated, because the port was filtered (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04). TRU says the agents failed where authentication was enforced, where paywalls required valid sessions and where endpoints were properly filtered, and that obscurity no longer protects a system from agents that investigate hundreds of targets at once (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04).

Exposure
Emergency-service, dispatch and public-safety systems that expose a record API or a legacy data port without authentication, leave default administrator credentials on a vendor's database panel, or ship secrets in front-end JavaScript; those are the weaknesses the agents turned into data, and TRU reports the patient-care and dispatch records as the gravest confirmed harm.
Detection
TRU names sqlmap, nmap and nikto among the most-used tools, so the traffic is ordinary scanner traffic in web access and authentication logs (an inference from the tool list): bursts of SQL-injection probing, repeated sign-in attempts against a single sign-on portal from one source, and logins to a database administration panel with a default account.
Defender takeaway
Swiss dispatch, patient-care and records systems of emergency services are the same target class, so check them for unauthenticated APIs and legacy ports, default root or administrator credentials on vendor panels, and keys or tokens in front-end code; the agents failed wherever authentication was enforced, so closing those gaps is what stops this tooling.

item.title: Brotli flaw hits Desigo CC, Industrial Edge and Mitel; Cisco lists Duo; Mitel and Common Configurator fixes pending
item.description: Between 2026-10-27 and 2026-11-06 Siemens, Mitel and Cisco listed affected products in advisories that cover the Brotli decoder flaw CVE-2026-111497: Siemens names Desigo CC V8 and V9 (remedy: the latest .NET security updates) and Industrial Edge, where Common Configurator has no fix; Mitel names MiVoice Business and five OpenScape products with updates planned and workaround articles for three; Cisco's combined advisory lists Duo Network Gateway (3.4.2) and RoomOS among its products with fixes, a longer list of which is dated up to 2027, without saying which of its CVEs each fix addresses. Cisco says it is not aware of malicious use against any Cisco product, and CISA lists the flaw as exploited.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-111497exploitedNATOA2

CVE-2026-111497, Brotli decoder flaw in Siemens Desigo CC and Industrial Edge, Mitel MiVoice Business and OpenScape, with Cisco listing Duo Network Gateway and RoomOS in its combined advisory: Desigo CC takes the .NET updates, while Mitel updates and the Industrial Edge Common Configurator fix are still pending

The Brotli decoder flaw CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write caused by improper handling of malformed compressed data (Mitel, 2026-10-28), and CISA lists it as exploited (CISA, 2026-10-27). Siemens' advisory SSA-045512, revised on 2026-11-06, lists Desigo CC V8 and V9, all versions, remedied by installing the latest .NET security updates via Windows Update, and scores the flaw CVSS 3.1 9.8 (Siemens ProductCERT, 2026-10-30). Its Industrial Edge advisory SSA-443410 says an Industrial Edge Management setup with no Management Applications installed needs no action because the affected functionality is not used or exposed, gives fixed versions for six configurator and monitoring applications, and for Common Configurator, which has no fix, says to uninstall all Management Applications and protect the instance with a firewall or WAF, or on a device to stop the application, until a fix is available (Siemens ProductCERT, 2026-10-30).

Mitel's MISA-2026-0010, revision 5.0 of 2026-11-04, rates the flaw high (CVSS 3.1 8.1) and lists MiVoice Business 10.6.0.7 and earlier, its Solution Virtual Instance up to the build in Mitel's table, OpenScape SBC V11R3.4.4 and earlier, OpenScape SESAP V2 R1.1.9 and earlier, OpenScape Contact Center V12R0 to V12R0FR7, OpenScape Xpert V9 R0.2.0 and earlier and OpenScape Endpoint Management V1 R2.5.1 and earlier as affected; for each an update is planned, not released, and workaround articles exist for OpenScape SBC, SESAP and Contact Center (Mitel, 2026-10-28). Mitel rates the risk low for MiVoice Business, Xpert and Endpoint Management when deployed according to its guidelines, and still lists several products as under investigation (Mitel, 2026-10-28).

Cisco's advisory, version 1.8 of 2026-11-06 and revised often, says its PSIRT is aware that proof-of-concept exploit code is available and is not aware of any malicious use against any Cisco product; it lists Catalyst SD-WAN, IOS XE, IOS XR and Secure Firewall ASA, FMC and FTD as not impacted and Identity Services Engine as under investigation (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-27). Its one fix table for the advisory's four CVEs, with no column for which CVE a fix addresses, lists Duo Network Gateway (3.4.2), Spaces (24.22.1), RoomOS on Board, Desk and Room Series devices (on-premises 11.41.2.3 and 26.7.4.3) and a longer list whose fixes are dated November 2026 to July 2027 (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-27).

Exposure
A Desigo CC host, an Industrial Edge Management instance with Management Applications installed or a Common Configurator on an Edge device, a Mitel MiVoice Business or OpenScape system at the listed versions, or a Cisco Duo Network Gateway or RoomOS device that Cisco lists in its combined advisory, below the builds above. Mitel says the impact on its products may differ from its rating because of product architecture (Mitel, 2026-10-28), so the vendor tables are the check.
Defender takeaway
Install the current .NET updates on every Desigo CC host. On Industrial Edge, update the monitoring and configurator applications to the fixed versions and, where Common Configurator runs, uninstall all Management Applications or stop it on Edge devices until Siemens ships a fix. Apply Mitel's workaround articles for OpenScape SBC, SESAP and Contact Center while no update is released, update Duo Network Gateway to the 3.4.2 that Cisco's table lists, and re-read Cisco's advisory, revised often, before relying on a fix date; Cisco says it is not aware of malicious use against its products, while CISA lists the flaw as exploited.

item.title: SonicWall SSL VPN bypasses SAML MFA and CISA lists it exploited; upgrade Gen7 to 7.3.4-7013, Gen8 to 8.2.3-8015
item.description: SonicWall's advisory SNWLID-2026-0014 of 2026-11-06 fixes CVE-2026-19868, an SSLVPN authentication enforcement flaw (CVSS 3.1 7.1) that lets a user with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method bypass SAML, MFA enforced through SAML included, on Gen7 firewalls up to 7.3.3-7015 and Gen8 up to 8.2.2-8015 when SAML is enabled for SSLVPN logins. SonicWall says it investigated a report indicating potential exploitation and CISA lists the flaw as exploited; there is no workaround, and 7.3.4-7013 and 8.2.3-8015 fix it.
item.content:encoded:
HIGHCVE-2026-19868 +3exploitedNATOA2

CVE-2026-19868, SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN: valid credentials for an alternate authentication method bypass SAML and the MFA it enforces; SonicWall investigated a report of exploitation and CISA lists it as exploited (CVSS 3.1 7.1)

SonicWall's advisory SNWLID-2026-0014 of 2026-11-06 fixes seven SonicOS flaws on Gen7 and Gen8 firewalls, and one of them, CVE-2026-19868, is an authentication enforcement weakness in the SSLVPN service: a user with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method may bypass the SAML authentication controls, and successful exploitation may also bypass SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-06). SonicWall says the flaw only affects SSLVPN when SAML is enabled for SSLVPN logins, and scores it CVSS 3.1 7.1 as a use of single-factor authentication (CWE-308) (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-06). The advisory says SonicWall PSIRT "has investigated a report indicating potential exploitation" and urges customers to upgrade, with no workaround available (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-06); CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-06 "based on evidence of active exploitation" (CISA, 2026-11-06). SonicWall has not shared details about the reported exploitation (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-06).

The advisory applies one table to all seven flaws: Gen7 hardware firewalls (TZ, NSa and NSsp) and Gen7 NSv up to and including 7.3.3-7015 are fixed in 7.3.4-7013 and higher, and Gen8 hardware firewalls (TZ and NSa) and Gen8 NSv up to and including 8.2.2-8015 are fixed in 8.2.3-8015 and higher (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-06). It also fixes two management-interface flaws scored 8.8 that in specific conditions could potentially let a remote unauthenticated attacker perform unauthorized operations, and that need user interaction, a pre-authentication heap overflow in the SSL-VPN service that could cause a denial of service, and three lower-severity flaws; no source reports them exploited (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-06).

Exposure
A Gen7 or Gen8 SonicWall firewall or NSv at or below the builds above with the SSL VPN enabled and SAML configured as a login method for SSLVPN; the running SonicOS build is the first check and the SAML setting for SSLVPN the second, the vendor's stated precondition (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-06).
Detection
The advisory gives no indicators. From the stated mechanism, compare successful SSLVPN logins on the firewall with the identity provider's sign-in log: a VPN session with no matching SAML sign-in or MFA event, or a SAML-enrolled user who authenticated through another authentication method, is the signal. Patching does not evict an attacker who already holds a session or reuses the credentials, so review VPN sessions since SAML was enabled and reset the credentials of accounts that work through both authentication methods.

Triage: a legitimate SAML sign-in leaves an event at the identity provider; a login through the alternate path does not, which follows from the stated mechanism.

Defender takeaway
Upgrade every Gen7 and Gen8 firewall that serves SAML SSLVPN logins to 7.3.4-7013 or 8.2.3-8015 or later now, because there is no workaround and the exploitation evidence is a vendor-investigated report plus CISA's listing; then review VPN sessions for logins that skipped the identity provider.

item.title: Update: Refrigeration attacks reach Switzerland, a Köniz butcher and three Volg stores; no actor established
item.description: NCSC Switzerland updated its advisory on 2026-11-06 with the Swiss incidents, Copeland and Dixell XWEB and healthcare, a four-point checklist for refrigeration management systems across all relevant operations, supplier-managed equipment included, and the statement that the public information does not establish a common attack method or confirm exploitation of the Danfoss CVEs it lists. Ransom-ISAC published the event log of one internet-reachable Copeland XWEB Pro compromise (743 parameter writes in two administrator sessions, default credentials claimed without published evidence), and Unit 42 counts over 5,000 exposed devices across countries on 5 and 6 November and a falling count in France since October.
item.content:encoded:
Update07 Nov 2026 03:53 UTCrun 2026-11-07T0256Z-intelsummaryactionssourcesevidencesourcing_note

NCSC Switzerland updated its advisory on 2026-11-06 with the Swiss incidents, Copeland and Dixell XWEB and healthcare, a four-point checklist for refrigeration management systems across all relevant operations, supplier-managed equipment included, and the statement that the public information does not establish a common attack method or confirm exploitation of the Danfoss CVEs it lists. Ransom-ISAC published the event log of one internet-reachable Copeland XWEB Pro compromise (743 parameter writes in two administrator sessions, default credentials claimed without published evidence), and Unit 42 counts over 5,000 exposed devices across countries on 5 and 6 November and a falling count in France since October.

NCSC Switzerland edited its advisory on 2026-11-06 with the reason "added Swiss incidents, Copeland/Dixell XWEB and healthcare attacks" and states that "The public information reviewed does not establish a common attack method across these incidents or confirm exploitation of the specific Danfoss CVEs listed above"; it lists CVE-2025-41451, CVE-2025-41450 and CVE-2025-41452 as "alleged as potentially related" (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13). Its checklist asks operators to review refrigeration management systems across all relevant operations, "including equipment managed by external service providers"; to remove direct internet access to management interfaces and provide remote access through a secure VPN; to check temperature settings, defrost schedules, alarm thresholds, notification recipients and user accounts, verify actual temperatures and test alarm delivery; and to apply current firmware and plan to replace equipment that no longer gets security updates (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13). For a suspected compromise it says "A factory reset alone is insufficient if the system remains vulnerable and directly accessible from the internet" (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13).

Ransom-ISAC published the event log of a Copeland XWEB Pro controller, reportedly on firmware 1.9.0 and reachable through a public address, compromised on 2 November: two Administrator sessions from different external addresses read parameters across 31 devices, then made 588 writes across 26 devices in about six minutes, which Ransom-ISAC reads as scripted or bulk programming rather than manual edits, and 155 further writes across five cold rooms, moving setpoints to 110 and 150 degrees C and recording keypad-lock, alarm-mute and defrost commands (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-06). The post says the controller still used its default Administrator credentials, publishes no evidence for that statement, says the log cannot show how the attackers got in or what temperatures were reached, and says it has no evidence linking the case to NoName057(16), Z-Pentest Alliance or the French attacks (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-06). Its suggested alerts are more than about 20 parameter-write events a minute from one account, writes to more than three devices within five minutes, and keypad-lock, alarm-mute or defrost commands that do not come from the scheduler (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-06).

Unit 42 counts over 5,000 internet-exposed devices across countries from the manufacturers CERT-FR names on 5 and 6 November, and for France alone 1,853 in the first half of October, 558 in the second half and 316 in the first six days of November, and says the claims of NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance remain unverified (Unit 42, 2026-11-06). The counts do not show which versions are vulnerable.

Open finding: Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb refrigeration controllers compromised, with forced defrost at hundreds of French supermarkets, refrigeration failures at more than 115 shops in at least six more countries and first cases in Germany, and on 2026-11-02 altered settings in the cold rooms of the French blood service through a refrigeration supplier, and on 2026-11-05 the first publicly known cases in Switzerland; responsibility not established; ENISA and Europol call for immediate action →

item.title: Update: CISA lists WordPress core's upgrade-window RCE race as exploited; block wp-content/upgrade before installing 7.1.4
item.description: The discoverer, Umut Bayram of Picus Security, shows that the update installing WordPress 7.1.4 still unpacks with the site's old code, so the staging folder under wp-content/upgrade can be reachable at a predictable path during that update, while a partial package exposes the installer only if it contains the installer files; he advises denying web access to the folder and confirming it answers 403 before updating.
item.content:encoded:
Update07 Nov 2026 03:51 UTCrun 2026-11-07T0256Z-intelheadlinesummaryactionssourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

The discoverer, Umut Bayram of Picus Security, shows that the update installing WordPress 7.1.4 still unpacks with the site's old code, so the staging folder under wp-content/upgrade can be reachable at a predictable path during that update, while a partial package exposes the installer only if it contains the installer files; he advises denying web access to the folder and confirming it answers 403 before updating.

Umut Bayram of Picus Security, who found the flaw, shows that the update which installs the fix still unpacks its files with the site's old, unpatched code (Picus Security, 2026-11-05; The Hacker News, 2026-11-06). Picus says the new code's skip of wp-config.php already works in that first update but the randomised folder name does not, so the temporary installer sits at a predictable path on sites running 5.9 or later and, on 4.4 to 5.8, behind a random suffix that hides it unless the site leaks the path; an attacker who reaches it can no longer replace the live configuration but can still set up the temporary copy, log in to it, run PHP and from there read or write files in the live directory (Picus Security, 2026-11-05). Bayram told The Hacker News the deciding factor "isn’t partial versus complete. It’s whether the updater already installed on the site has been fixed", and that a partial package exposes the installer only if it contains the installer files; The Hacker News found WordPress.org offering an in-branch move such as 7.1.3 to 7.1.4 as a partial package, automatic updates included, so whether such an update is exposed depends on what that package contains, and only once 7.1.4 or the branch fix is installed do later updates use a random folder (The Hacker News, 2026-11-06). WordPress 4.6 and earlier get no fix (The Hacker News, 2026-11-06).

The order matters: Picus advises denying web access to wp-content/upgrade/ in the web server configuration first, confirming that the path answers 403, and only then updating; this does not break updates, because WordPress reaches the folder through the filesystem (Picus Security, 2026-11-05). An .htaccess file placed inside the folder does not work, because the old updater deletes the folder's contents before unpacking, and WP-CLI's wp core update is no substitute because it uses the same updater and folder (Picus Security, 2026-11-05). For sites that stayed on an affected version, Wordfence suggests looking for unexpected requests to PHP files under wp-content/upgrade, administrator accounts no one recognises, plugins no one installed and PHP files in wp-content/upgrade that no one put there (The Hacker News, 2026-11-06).

Code that its authors describe as an exploit has appeared in public GitHub repositories since earlier this week, and whether it works has not been established; WordPress's own advisory rates the flaw low, against Wordfence's CVSS 8.1 and CISA's listing as exploited (The Hacker News, 2026-11-06). None of these sources reports a compromise through the update that installs the fix; CISA's listing and Wordfence's probing telemetry above are unchanged.

Open finding: WordPress core 4.7 to 7.1.3: an unauthenticated race in the core update process can lead to remote code execution, fixed in 7.1.4 and backported to every supported branch, listed by CISA as exploited; Wordfence assigned CVE-2026-119977 →

item.title: Update: Microsoft: Storm-0940 runs ARTEX at machine speed; Mandiant now sees agent frameworks in incident-response cases
item.description: Microsoft reports that Storm-3358, a Cambodia-based, financially motivated cluster, has used ARTEX since October 2026 against financial organisations, pairing it with conventional scanners and installing the open-source remote access tools WISP, vshell and AdaptixC2; Check Point Research reads ten exposed operator consoles showing campaigns that run almost autonomously once a goal is set, and Microsoft says honeypots, decoys, tarpits and fake wins helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets.
item.content:encoded:
Update07 Nov 2026 03:50 UTCrun 2026-11-07T0256Z-intelsummaryentitiestechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_note

Microsoft reports that Storm-3358, a Cambodia-based, financially motivated cluster, has used ARTEX since October 2026 against financial organisations, pairing it with conventional scanners and installing the open-source remote access tools WISP, vshell and AdaptixC2; Check Point Research reads ten exposed operator consoles showing campaigns that run almost autonomously once a goal is set, and Microsoft says honeypots, decoys, tarpits and fake wins helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence reports that Storm-3358, a Cambodia-based intrusion cluster that primarily targets financial organisations in Southeast Asia and a smaller number of large financial organisations globally, began using ARTEX against the financial sector in October 2026 (Microsoft, 2026-11-06). Microsoft says the cluster combines ARTEX with conventional automated tools to scan internet-facing systems, exploit flaws including anonymous file upload and server-side request forgery, and install the open-source remote access tools WISP, vshell and AdaptixC2, which ARTEX agents download with netcat and curl (Microsoft, 2026-11-06). Microsoft's tell for an agent on a scanned system is "a wide variety of requests in a brief time", retries of variations on one technique and a move to next-stage actions at machine speed; ARTEX by default drives Nmap, curl, wget, Python HTTP clients and headless Chromium through Playwright, and blocking their default traits will not stop an agent, which "will quickly change them" (Microsoft, 2026-11-06). In Microsoft's testing, honeypots, decoys, tarpits and fake wins helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets, with no figures given (Microsoft, 2026-11-06).

Check Point Research counts 2,557 systems that host or hosted ARTEX panels, 1,608 of them live and public, and ten that exposed the full database; in those ten consoles the operators set a goal and then "barely interacted with their agent fleets" (Check Point, 2026-11-05). The campaigns it reads are opportunistic crime, not espionage: iOS signing certificates from grey-market shops, a cryptocurrency-service campaign and game-account credentials. In the signing-shop campaign the agents got in through hardcoded administrator passwords in JavaScript bundles, missing API authentication, command injection, insecure direct object references, weak administrative credentials and template injection (Check Point, 2026-11-05). Check Point does not name Storm-3358.

Open finding: ARTEX: Microsoft reports Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, running an open-source multi-agent LLM penetration-testing framework against hundreds of organizations, with privileged cloud access in under three hours in some cases, and Expel sees the same infrastructure abuse Okta self-service registration →

item.title: Update: Cisco's mail gateway can be rooted by one crafted email; found in a TAC support case, exploitation confirmed
item.description: Rapid7's Metasploit framework now carries public modules for two unauthenticated SQL injections on Cisco Secure Email Gateway that end in root command execution: one merged on 2026-11-05 for the injection its author matches, at medium confidence, to the exploited CVE-2026-76461 and which needs URL Filtering and URL Retrospective Service enabled, and one for the non-default S/MIME public-key harvesting feature that Rapid7 believes is CVE-2026-76443. A clean mail_logs check does not rule out the S/MIME injection, and Cisco's hardening advisory names no fixed 16.0 build.
item.content:encoded:
Update07 Nov 2026 03:49 UTCrun 2026-11-07T0256Z-intelsummarycvesactionssourcesevidencesourcing_notebodytagsimmediate_action

Rapid7's Metasploit framework now carries public modules for two unauthenticated SQL injections on Cisco Secure Email Gateway that end in root command execution: one merged on 2026-11-05 for the injection its author matches, at medium confidence, to the exploited CVE-2026-76461 and which needs URL Filtering and URL Retrospective Service enabled, and one for the non-default S/MIME public-key harvesting feature that Rapid7 believes is CVE-2026-76443. A clean mail_logs check does not rule out the S/MIME injection, and Cisco's hardening advisory names no fixed 16.0 build.

Rapid7's Metasploit framework now carries public exploit modules for two unauthenticated SQL injections on Cisco Secure Email Gateway that end in command execution as root. The first, merged on 2026-11-05, targets an injection in the Email Cloud Scanner URL-retrospective message database and its documentation says "URL Filtering and URL Retrospective Service must both be enabled" (Rapid7 Metasploit module documentation, 2026-10-16), which sits against Cisco's statement that the flaw affects the gateway "regardless of device configuration" (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-09-14); its author says it can only be assessed with medium confidence that this is CVE-2026-76461, the flaw CISA lists, and that of the injections reproduced from the patch diff it was the only one that left the pattern COPY.*TO PROGRAM in mail_logs, the check Cisco's own advisory names (Rapid7 Metasploit pull request 22024, 2026-10-16). The second targets an injection in the S/MIME public-key harvesting feature, "we have reason to believe this maps to CVE-2026-76443" according to Rapid7's wrap-up of 2026-11-06 (Rapid7, 2026-11-06). The S/MIME module was merged on 2026-10-28; its author tested a gateway on AsyncOS 15.5.1-055 with the S/MIME Public Key Harvesting feature enabled for inbound mail, and the module sends one signed S/MIME email carrying 500 certificate addresses to the gateway's SMTP listener (Rapid7 Metasploit pull request 22018, 2026-10-15). Its documentation says "Public-key harvesting must be enabled on the inbound mail flow policy for the target to be exploitable" (Rapid7 Metasploit module documentation, 2026-10-15), and the author of the first module calls that feature "a different non-default feature" (Rapid7 Metasploit pull request 22024, 2026-10-16).

Cisco's hardening advisory lists CVE-2026-76443 with the other grouped CVEs and its fixed-release table gives 15.5.5-014 for 15.5 and earlier, 16.5.0-780 for 16.5 and "Migrate to a fixed release." for 16.0 (Cisco PSIRT, hardening-release advisory, 2026-09-14). A 16.0 appliance on 16.0.4-302 therefore has no named fix for the flaw the S/MIME module most likely uses; moving to 16.5.0-780 closes it. Rapid7 does not report exploitation of the S/MIME module's flaw, and Cisco does not say whether the injection it lists as exploited is the one in either module.

Open finding: CVE-2026-76461: Cisco Secure Email Gateway unauthenticated SQL injection in email parsing reaches root command execution, exploited before disclosure (CVSS 9.8) →

item.title: Qilin's October build spreads through vCenter and ESXi, reboots into Safe Mode and prints notes on office printers
item.description: Seqrite compares a March 2026 and an October 2026 Qilin (Agenda) sample and reports that the newer build embeds a PowerShell engine that logs in to vCenter, disables HA and DRS and pushes Linux payloads to ESXi hosts over SSH, shuts down the processes that lock files through the Windows Restart Manager instead of brute-force termination, sets a Safe Mode reboot so EDR drivers do not load, and sends ransom notes to TCP 9100 on local subnets. It is a vendor analysis of two samples with no incident confirmation.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB3

Seqrite: reverse engineering of two Qilin builds shows the October 2026 variant adding a vCenter and ESXi spreading engine, Restart Manager lock release, a Safe Mode reboot loop and ransom notes printed to office printers

Seqrite's reverse engineering of a March 2026 and an October 2026 Qilin (Agenda) sample finds that the Rust code was reworked into a modular workspace of 22 internal crates, that the command line grew from 6 to 42 switches, and that the October build carries subsystems the baseline lacked (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03). It uses the Windows Restart Manager API to shut down the processes that lock SQL Server, Exchange and virtual-machine disk files, instead of the brute-force process termination of the March sample, so that the files can be encrypted (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03). An embedded PowerShell engine, started with --spread-vcenter, authenticates to vCenter, disables HA and DRS, extracts the ESXi host addresses, opens SSH and SCP sessions, uploads Linux ransomware payloads to /tmp on the hosts and runs esxcli to power off virtual machines and encrypt .vmdk volumes (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03).

The build also installs the RSAT Active Directory module itself with DISM before enumerating computers, embeds 32-bit and 64-bit PsExec to spread over the ADMIN$ and C$ shares with harvested credentials, and sets a Safe Mode boot with bcdedit plus an AutoAdminLogon registry value so that it reboots into Safe Mode, where EDR drivers do not load (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03). A raw-printing module scans local subnets for TCP port 9100 and sends cleartext ransom notes to office printers, and the October binary masquerades as resmon.exe with a forged Microsoft code-signing overlay (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03). Seqrite lists healthcare, manufacturing, education and technology as the victim sectors in its telemetry (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03).

Exposure
Windows estates with a vCenter and ESXi hosts that a domain-joined host can reach over the network and SSH, since the spreading engine needs a vCenter login and SSH to the hosts; Seqrite names no initial-access route.
Detection
In vCenter audit events, HA or DRS being disabled on a cluster followed by SSH sessions to ESXi hosts and esxcli activity; in process-creation and registry telemetry, bcdedit setting a Safe Mode boot and a Winlogon AutoAdminLogon change outside a change window, DISM installing the RSAT Active Directory component on a host that never had it, and rstrtmgr.dll loaded by a process that is not an installer; in network telemetry, one host sending to TCP 9100 on many hosts of a subnet; and an executable named resmon.exe outside System32 (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03).

Triage: the Restart Manager and a DISM-installed RSAT component are normal in patching and administration, so each is weak alone; the combination with the print fan-out, the Safe Mode change and the vCenter actions is the signal.

Defender takeaway
Treat HA or DRS being turned off in vCenter, followed by SSH sessions to ESXi hosts, as an incident, and alert on a Safe Mode boot configured by bcdedit outside change windows, which Seqrite names as a detection point (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03).

item.title: Microsoft Q3 email report: overrides let authentication-failing spoofed mail through; SVG CAPTCHA phishing returns
item.description: Microsoft's Q3 2026 email-threat report finds that many malicious messages spoofing the sender domains of business services were delivered despite failing authentication because tenant- or user-level overrides applied, 63% of the messages with a recorded security outcome in September. It also reports SVG attachments leading CAPTCHA-gated phishing at quarter end, Teams impersonators shifting from help-desk display names to ordinary personal names, and an August device-code phishing campaign that used a QR code in a Word document against legal organisations.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

Microsoft Email Threat Landscape Q3 2026: tenant and user overrides delivered spoofed business-service mail that failed authentication, SVG attachments return as CAPTCHA-phishing carriers, and Teams impersonators move to ordinary personal names

Microsoft Threat Intelligence's report on Q3 2026 draws four points that matter to a Microsoft 365 defender (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05). First, malicious messages that spoof the sender domains of business services, such as document-signing and survey platforms, were often delivered because tenant- or user-level overrides applied, even after the messages failed email authentication and were identified as malicious: in September overrides applied to 63% of messages with a recorded security outcome, most of them tenant-level (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05). Microsoft says the figures do not show that recipients opened the messages and that an overly broad exception made for a legitimate workflow can weaken protection against messages impersonating it (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).

Second, CAPTCHA-gated phishing recovered while QR-code phishing kept falling, with SVG attachments central to the recovery: they carried 65% of CAPTCHA-gated attacks in August and 49% in September (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05). Third, in Teams, ordinary personal-name display names rose from 46% of the observed July sample to 88% in September while explicit help-desk identities fell from 17% to 2%; Microsoft notes a personal name can accompany a help-desk claim while the account address keeps technical wording, and that more targeted attempts used domains resembling the victim organisation's (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05). Fourth, an August campaign against legal organisations sent a Word document with a personalised QR code that led to a device-code phishing page and the genuine Microsoft device sign-in portal; completing the sign-in would have transferred a valid session token that gave persistent access without exposing the password or re-triggering MFA (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).

Exposure
A Microsoft 365 tenant that has tenant- or user-level allow or override entries covering the sender domains of widely used business services, since a message that fails authentication and is detected as malicious can still be delivered when such an override applies.
Detection
In mail-flow and message-trace telemetry, delivered messages that claim a business service's domain but fail SPF, DKIM and DMARC, together with the override that applied; in mail-gateway logs, SVG attachments that lead to a CAPTCHA page; in Teams audit, first-contact chats and calls from external tenants whose display name is a personal name but whose account address carries help-desk or service wording; in sign-in logs, device-code flow sign-ins.
Defender takeaway
Review the tenant and user overrides in your mail protection for entries that cover well-known service sender domains, because the override, not the detection, decided delivery; Microsoft's own advice is to check its recommended settings for Exchange Online Protection and Defender for Office 365 (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).

item.title: Entra app-credential abuse: agents hunt GitHub for secrets, an operator reaches MSP clients, government among them
item.description: Microsoft reports that since August threat actors have used the agentic framework ARTEX to query public GitHub for OAuth application secrets and cloud keys, and that from 2026-10-28 valid application credentials were used for service-principal sign-ins across dozens of applications in several tenants, a vendor-owned multitenant application among them. Todyl's telemetry shows one operator since 2026-11-01 targeting about 45 application registrations at MSPs, more than 33 of which authenticated, and reaching 27 organisations, government clients among them; Microsoft says a similar campaign involving the same addresses was reported by Todyl, while Todyl does not tie its case to ARTEX and cannot say where the secrets came from.
item.content:encoded:
HIGHNATOB2

Exposed application credentials: Microsoft sees an agentic framework search GitHub for OAuth and cloud application secrets and then sign in as the applications from 2026-10-28, and Todyl sees an operator use MSP applications to reach 27 organisations, government clients among them

Microsoft reports that since August 2026 threat actors have used the agentic offensive framework ARTEX to submit large volumes of queries to public GitHub for secrets (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05). As early as 2026-10-28 it saw successful service-principal sign-ins from two IP addresses, one a Tor exit node that may carry unrelated activity, across dozens of applications in several tenants, including a vendor-owned multitenant application whose credential was compromised at the source and used to reach multiple downstream tenants (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05). Microsoft states that a similar campaign involving the same addresses was also reported by Todyl (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).

Todyl, from its managed-detection telemetry, describes one operator who since 2026-11-01 has signed in to MSPs' Microsoft 365 and Azure environments as their own applications with stolen credentials that are still valid: about 45 app registrations at roughly 18 organisations were targeted, more than 33 authenticated, and 27 organisations were reached, among them the MSPs' downstream clients in government (Todyl, 2026-11-03). For nearly every credential the operator requests an Azure Resource Manager token, then a Key Vault token, and within minutes applications that had never been used start authenticating; MSP multitenant and delegated-admin apps and Partner Center tokens reach client tenants, one app sweeping 15 client tenants in about 10-second loops (Todyl, 2026-11-03). Todyl says no Microsoft vulnerability is involved, that it saw no persistence and does not know how the credentials were obtained, and that several seed secrets had only ever been used from staff devices and office networks, which points to a file store or live backend rather than configurations crawled from the internet (Todyl, 2026-11-03). After its detections fired on 2026-11-03 the operator switched to spoofed browser user agents and replayed users' refresh tokens, all blocked by Conditional Access (Todyl, 2026-11-03).

Exposure
Any Entra tenant, an MSP's or a customer's, that holds app registrations with client secrets, above all multitenant, delegated-admin and Partner Center applications and Azure DevOps service connections, security-tool integration apps among those abused (Todyl, 2026-11-03); Conditional Access for workload identities needs the Workload ID Premium licence and covers only single-tenant apps (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).
Detection
In Entra service-principal and non-interactive sign-in logs, an invalid-secret or expired-secret error for an application followed by a success, one address authenticating as service principals in several unrelated tenants within 24 hours, an Azure Resource Manager token followed at once by a Key Vault token and then by previously unused apps authenticating, and failed service-principal sign-ins from hosting space that never succeed, which success-only logic misses (Todyl, 2026-11-03). In Azure DevOps auditing, personal access token creation and first use, federated service connections and pipeline edits (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).

Triage: the invalid-secret and expired-secret errors alone only show that someone holds an old or wrong credential for the app; Microsoft treats a failure followed by a success as the urgent case (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).

Defender takeaway
Inventory the client secrets on app registrations and hunt the sign-in pattern above in every tenant you run or manage, MSP-managed communal tenants included; on an affected app remove every client secret, certificate and federated credential, including those the actor added, and rotate what any Key Vault it could read holds, because tokens already issued stay valid until expiry (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).

item.description: SRF reported on 2026-11-05 the first publicly known cases of the refrigeration attacks in Switzerland, a butcher in Köniz whose freezer reached 50 to 70 degrees and three Volg stores with changed cooling parameters; BACS has received one reportable notification about an attack on commercial refrigeration, and CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA and DOT published a joint fact sheet on refrigeration and cold-chain controllers that names no vendor, CVE or actor. item.content:encoded:
Update06 Nov 2026 03:44 UTCrun 2026-11-06T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

SRF reported on 2026-11-05 the first publicly known cases of the refrigeration attacks in Switzerland, a butcher in Köniz whose freezer reached 50 to 70 degrees and three Volg stores with changed cooling parameters; BACS has received one reportable notification about an attack on commercial refrigeration, and CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA and DOT published a joint fact sheet on refrigeration and cold-chain controllers that names no vendor, CVE or actor. No source names the controller make or the access route in the Swiss cases.

SRF reported on 2026-11-05 the first publicly known attack of this kind in Switzerland: the butcher Lüthis Fleischwaren in Köniz, canton Bern, told customers that manipulation of the electronic control of its cooling and freezer systems caused considerable temperature deviations, the owner told SRF he found 50 to 70 degrees in the freezer, and the firm disconnected the installation from the network and closed the branch (translated from German) (SRF, 2026-11-05). Keystone-SDA adds that the shop can probably only reopen on 20 November and that the Bern cantonal police were briefly informed on Monday and had received no complaint yet (Keystone-SDA via swissinfo.ch, 2026-11-05). Volg says three of its stores noticed that parameters in the cooling shelves had been changed (SRF, 2026-11-05). No source names the controller make, the access route or a maintenance provider in the Swiss cases; Keystone-SDA notes that operators can supervise cooling plants centrally over the internet and that the butcher apparently has such an installation, which is the agency's inference and not the owner's statement (Keystone-SDA via swissinfo.ch, 2026-11-05). BACS told Keystone-SDA that it does not comment on specific incidents and has received one reportable notification about a cyberattack on commercial refrigeration so far, and it stressed that voluntary reports are welcome at any time (Keystone-SDA via swissinfo.ch, 2026-11-05). Blutspende SRK Schweiz told Keystone-SDA that no attacks on Swiss blood-donation services are known to date (SRF, 2026-11-05).

On the same day CISA, the FBI, HHS, USDA and DOT published a joint fact sheet on malicious cyber activity against industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems worldwide: the actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, through authentication bypass, arbitrary code injection or weak configurations, with loss of visibility into current temperatures as a further effect (CISA, 2026-11-05). It names no vendor, CVE, victim or actor; its mitigations include keeping controller panels off the internet, allowlisting the devices and IP addresses that may change settings, defining reasonable setpoint limits for downstream devices with alerting on deviations, and collecting network traffic between OT assets where logs are not available (CISA, 2026-11-05).

Open finding: Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb refrigeration controllers compromised, with forced defrost at hundreds of French supermarkets, refrigeration failures at more than 115 shops in at least six more countries and first cases in Germany, and on 2026-11-02 altered settings in the cold rooms of the French blood service through a refrigeration supplier, and on 2026-11-05 the first publicly known cases in Switzerland; responsibility not established; ENISA and Europol call for immediate action →

item.title: Storm-2603-linked SharePoint intrusion: memory-only VirtualPathProvider shell in w3wp.exe, then Velociraptor and tunnels
item.description: Kaspersky's retrospective of a December intrusion at a customer's on-premises SharePoint server, which it attributes to Storm-2603 with moderate confidence, shows a ToolShell exploit that left no file on disk: a C# memory shell registered as an ASP.NET VirtualPathProvider inside the IIS worker process w3wp.exe, dormant until a specific User-Agent arrived, with an suo5 proxy that turned the SharePoint host into a pivot. The actor then installed an outdated Velociraptor and several tunnelling mechanisms so access outlived the worker process, and Kaspersky's endpoint product blocked the Warlock encryption attempt.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

Kaspersky reconstructs an intrusion through SharePoint ToolShell, attributed to Storm-2603 with moderate confidence, whose implant lived only inside w3wp.exe: an ASP.NET VirtualPathProvider memory shell with a suo5 tunnel, then Velociraptor, several tunnelling mechanisms and Warlock's AV killer

Kaspersky's retrospective analysis of a December intrusion at a customer's on-premises SharePoint server found activity consistent with Storm-2603, with the access and control layer held entirely inside the IIS worker process w3wp.exe and nothing written to disk (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). On December 20 a single request to a SharePoint administrative endpoint tied to the ToolPane component fingerprinted the host for ToolShell (CVE-2025-53770); the full exploit chain ran on December 24 against the same endpoint, and the gap kept the probe from being correlated with it (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). The payload was loaded into the ASP.NET runtime and lost when the application pool recycled or IIS restarted (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05).

The memory shell registers a custom VirtualPathProvider through a non-public method of the ASP.NET HostingEnvironment class, subverts trust controls so that the registration works even in a precompiled application, intercepts requests at the GetCacheKey() hook and stays dormant unless a specific User-Agent header arrives (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). It speaks a custom XOR-obfuscated binary protocol, and the open-source suo5 tool proxies traffic so connections from the command server reach arbitrary hosts inside the network through the SharePoint server (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). It reaches SYSTEM by named-pipe token impersonation adapted from EfsPotato and creates administrative accounts through native SAM RPC calls (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05).

Shortly after the injection w3wp.exe started msiexec.exe to install a remote MSI that was Velociraptor 0.73.4.0, vulnerable to CVE-2025-6264, which the actor used for persistence, discovery, data collection and payload execution and to deploy Zoho Assist unattended access, a VS Code CLI tunnel, Cloudflare Tunnel and a reverse proxy, so access no longer depended on the IIS process (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). The actor then uploaded a vulnerable driver that is used to terminate EDR products and sideloaded a DLL that Kaspersky identified as Warlock ransomware's AV killer, possibly meant to use that driver; Kaspersky's endpoint product blocked the ransomware process (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05).

Exposure
An internet-reachable on-premises SharePoint Server on which ToolShell (CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-53771) is exploitable (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05).
Detection
In CLR loader telemetry, a dynamically compiled App_Web_toolpane assembly and a Microsoft.GeneratedCode assembly loading in the same application domain after a ToolPane request; in the IIS-Configuration ETW provider, events 25 and 47 for a path without the file-change-monitor events 17, 18, 19 and 21 that a real file produces, checked against an allow-list of legitimate VirtualPathProvider implementations; and memory inspection of w3wp.exe (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05).

Triage: App_Web_* assemblies come from ordinary ASP.NET page compilation and Microsoft.GeneratedCode from legitimate XmlSerializer use, so neither is a signal alone; the signal is the pair in one application domain right after a ToolPane request, and any VirtualPathProvider that is not on the application's inventory (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). The December 20 probe came from infrastructure associated with ONYPHE, an attack-surface discovery platform whose vulnerability checks use non-intrusive probes, so a probe alone looks like a benign scanner; Kaspersky's retrospective analysis established the probe as the initial phase of the intrusion that followed on the same endpoint (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05).

Defender takeaway
On a SharePoint host that shows a code-execution exploit, contain the host, hunt the persistence that was installed afterwards, and rotate credentials and the exposed ASP.NET MachineKey; removing the initial shell or known indicators is not enough (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). Hunt for VirtualPathProvider implants with the ETW pattern above on SharePoint farms that were exposed to ToolShell.

Builds on: Symantec: Warlock's operator steals SharePoint machine keys, forges signed payloads and ships…

item.title: FreeSWITCH: one SIP MESSAGE runs API commands, vendor says exploited; fixed in 1.11.3
item.description: SignalWire's advisory of 2026-10-28 describes CVE-2026-116779 (CVSS 3.1 9.8): an inbound SIP MESSAGE to a FreeSWITCH SIP profile selects the api chat proto and runs FreeSWITCH API commands with the privileges of the FreeSWITCH process, in the default configuration of 1.11.2 and earlier, and the advisory states that exploitation of this path has been observed in the wild. BSI CERT-Bund relayed it as a critical advisory on 2026-11-05; no source names an actor or victim, and the exploitation claim is the vendor's alone.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-116779exploitedNATOA2

CVE-2026-116779, FreeSWITCH 1.11.2 and earlier: one inbound SIP MESSAGE can select the api chat proto and run FreeSWITCH API commands, the vendor says exploitation has been observed, and 1.11.3 fixes it (CVSS 3.1 9.8)

SignalWire's advisory GHSA-mg63-h38w-8p9p describes CVE-2026-116779: FreeSWITCH's sofia_presence_handle_sip_i_message() splits the To user of an inbound SIP MESSAGE on + and treats the left half as a chat proto name, the mod_dptools module registers an api chat interface that hands its address to switch_api_execute(), and a peer that can deliver a MESSAGE to a profile therefore selects which FreeSWITCH API command the server runs (SignalWire, 2026-10-28). The impact is command execution with the privileges of the FreeSWITCH process, including arbitrary operating-system commands, disclosure of configuration and credentials and full call control, and where mod_lua is loaded, as the stock configuration does, inline Lua is a second route (SignalWire, 2026-10-28). The advisory scores it CVSS 3.1 9.8, lists 1.11.2 and earlier as affected and 1.11.3 as patched, and states that exploitation of this path has been observed in the wild without naming an actor or a victim (SignalWire, 2026-10-28). BSI CERT-Bund rated its advisory on the flaw critical and lists versions before 1.11.3 as affected (BSI CERT-Bund, 2026-11-05).

The default posture is exposed: chat handling is on unless a profile sets enable-chat=false, the stock vanilla configuration leaves it on for the internal and external profiles, and the inbound ACL does not cover MESSAGE; where MESSAGE authentication is enforced (the default from 1.10.7) any one account on the profile is enough, and installations that still carry the sample directory user default, which has no password, need no account of their own (SignalWire, 2026-10-28). The fix is a per-profile enable-chat-api-proto parameter that is off unless set, so the route is closed by default and a MESSAGE that selects the proto is answered with 403 and logged with the source and the requested command (SignalWire, 2026-10-28). auth-messages alone does not close the path, and disable_system_api_commands=true removes the system API but leaves the route to every other registered API, module loading and call origination included (SignalWire, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A FreeSWITCH of version 1.11.2 or earlier with a SIP profile that accepts inbound MESSAGE from a peer that can reach it, which is the default configuration (SignalWire, 2026-10-28).
Detection
SIP signalling logs, or packet capture at the session border controller, for MESSAGE requests whose To user carries a + with api as the left half, in any letter case; after the upgrade the 403 and the log line with the source and the requested command mark attempts (SignalWire, 2026-10-28). The mechanism also implies child processes such as a shell or a downloader started by the FreeSWITCH process, and, where an instance was reachable before the fix, changes to its Lua scripts, dialplan or loaded modules.
Defender takeaway
Upgrade to 1.11.3, or until then set enable-chat=false on every profile that does not need inbound SIP chat and remove directory users that have no password; on an instance that was reachable by SIP peers, treat its configuration and the credentials it holds as disclosed, because the vendor says exploitation has been observed (SignalWire, 2026-10-28).

item.title: Update: Barracuda ESG: no login needed, watchTowr shows one request reaches root; update to 9.4.0.029 or later
item.description: watchTowr Labs published the full chain on 2026-11-05 and a detection tool: one unauthenticated request to the Email Security Gateway's login handler reaches the backup-restore function, a secret that is hard-coded in the product lets an attacker build a valid archive, and the restored timezone value reaches the root command injection, so exploitation needs no account; Barracuda changed its own advisory the same day to say authentication is not required for CVE-2026-116606. No source reports attacks.
item.content:encoded:
Update06 Nov 2026 03:41 UTCrun 2026-11-06T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummaryprioritytagscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

watchTowr Labs published the full chain on 2026-11-05 and a detection tool: one unauthenticated request to the Email Security Gateway's login handler reaches the backup-restore function, a secret that is hard-coded in the product lets an attacker build a valid archive, and the restored timezone value reaches the root command injection, so exploitation needs no account; Barracuda changed its own advisory the same day to say authentication is not required for CVE-2026-116606. No source reports attacks.

watchTowr Labs published the full chain on 2026-11-05 after comparing firmware 9.4.0.027 with 9.4.0.029 (watchTowr Labs, 2026-11-05). In the login handler a failed password-change attempt returns the login-screen role instead of ending the request, so one unauthenticated POST to /cgi-mod/index.cgi that submits mismatching new and retyped passwords with a backup upload reaches the backup-restore function (watchTowr Labs, 2026-11-05). The restore accepts a backup whose checksum matches, and the checksum is built from the file bytes and a secret that is hard-coded in the product, so an attacker can build a valid archive (watchTowr Labs, 2026-11-05). A restored system_timezone value then reaches an unescaped shell call that runs as root (watchTowr Labs, 2026-11-05). watchTowr shares a Detection Artefact Generator so that owners can test their own appliances, and its post does not claim exploitation in the wild (watchTowr Labs, 2026-11-05). Its README describes a tool that takes a target URL and a command, builds a backup, uploads it to the target and attempts to check whether the target is vulnerable (watchTowr Labs README, 2026-11-03).

Barracuda changed its advisory the same day, 2026-11-05 at 2:30pm EST: the Authentication Required field for CVE-2026-116606 now reads No (Administrative UI Access Required), and the advisory says authentication is not required to exploit it but the administrative user interface must be accessible to the attacker (Barracuda, 2026-11-05). The advisory's entry for CVE-2026-111560 still reads Yes (Administrative Access) (Barracuda, 2026-11-05).

Open finding: CVE-2026-116606 / CVE-2026-111560, Barracuda Email Security Gateway: an unauthenticated configuration-import bypass chained with a root command injection, with watchTowr's full chain and a detection tool public since 2026-11-05; patches are out and no exploitation is reported (CVSS 9.3 and 8.6) →

item.title: OpenSSH 10.6p2: password bypass on musl Linux without PAM (Alpine, OpenWrt); update or turn passwords off
item.description: OpenSSH Portable 10.6p2 of 2026-11-05 works around CVE-2026-123158, a password-authentication bypass on Linux systems that use musl libc and run sshd without PAM, Alpine's default OpenSSH server and OpenWrt among them: a password of 257 to 1,024 bytes logs in to an account whose password field is *. NCSC Switzerland published an advisory the same day and rates exploitation unknown; Alpine shipped fixed packages for every branch back to 3.16. Previdian's page, as read on 2026-11-07, reports 15 exploitation attempts from 10 addresses since 2026-11-06 and, according to The Hacker News, a successful root login on an Alpine honeypot; CISA does not list the flaw.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-123158updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-123158, OpenSSH Portable before 10.6p2 (*sshole): on Linux with musl libc and no PAM, a password of 257 to 1,024 bytes logs in to accounts whose password field is *; NCSC Switzerland issued an advisory (CVSS 3.1 8.1)

Portable OpenSSH 10.6p2 carries what its release notes call a critical security workaround for Linux systems that use the musl libc with PAM disabled (OpenSSH, 2026-11-05). NCSC Switzerland says remote, unauthenticated attackers can bypass SSH password authentication over the network and gain access, and rated the exploitation status unknown (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-05). OX Security explains the mechanism: musl's crypt() refuses inputs over 256 bytes and returns the string * when it fails, * is also what /etc/shadow holds for an account with no valid password, and OpenSSH, whose 2016 user-enumeration countermeasure can hash a password with settings taken from another account, reads the two matching values as a successful login (OX Security, 2026-11-05). OX gives the conditions: sshd on musl without PAM (Alpine's openssh-server by default), password logins enabled, an account whose password field is * (key-only users, LDAP users, root on Alpine) and at least one other account on the host with a real password; accounts that hold !, glibc systems, PAM setups, Dropbear and OpenBSD are not affected, and OX scores the flaw CVSS 3.1 8.1 (OX Security, 2026-11-05). On Alpine's official AWS and Azure images the passwordless account is the default alpine user, which can run doas without a password, so the bypass chains to root (OX Security, 2026-11-05); Alpine says those tiny-cloud images are safe on first boot and exploitable once any $6$ hash exists, and that cloud-init images, which write PasswordAuthentication no, are not affected (Alpine Linux, 2026-11-05).

The OpenSSH developers do not consider the root cause to lie in OpenSSH (heise online, 2026-11-05), and NCSC Switzerland adds that other software with similar authentication paths may be affected (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-05). Alpine pushed the fix to every branch back to 3.16 (OX Security, 2026-11-05); on release day other distributions and many OpenSSH download servers still offered 10.6p1 (heise online, 2026-11-05).

Exposure
Sshd on a musl-based Linux system built without PAM, which NCSC Switzerland lists as Alpine, KISS, Sabotage, OpenWrt, Morpheus and other musl distributions that do not use PAM for password authentication, with password logins enabled (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-05) and, per OX Security, an account whose /etc/shadow password field is * (OX Security, 2026-11-05). Containers that do not run an OpenSSH server are not affected (OX Security, 2026-11-05).
Detection
OX Security advises searching /var/log/messages for Accepted password for on an account that has no password (alpine, root, key-only users) and treating the machine as compromised if one is found (OX Security, 2026-11-05). The mechanism implies the same event in any sshd authentication log; no source publishes an indicator beyond that.

Triage: an accepted password login is normal for an account with a real hash; the same event for an account whose password field is * has no benign explanation, because such an account cannot match any password.

Defender takeaway
Install OpenSSH 10.6p2 or the distribution's fixed package on every musl-based host that runs sshd and restart sshd, because updating the package alone does not replace the SSH server that is already running, and rebuild container and cloud images from a fixed base (OX Security, 2026-11-05); until then set PasswordAuthentication no and restart sshd, as NCSC Switzerland advises (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-05). Review the accepted password logins for key-only accounts on every musl host that allowed password logins before patching, now that exploitation attempts are reported.
Update07 Nov 2026 03:52 UTCrun 2026-11-07T0256Z-intelsummarytagscvesevidencesourcessourcing_notebody

Previdian's page for CVE-2026-123158, as read on 2026-11-07, says its sensors observed 15 exploitation attempts from 10 addresses in 8 countries, first on 2026-11-06 and last on 2026-11-07, a live counter, and that these observations do not show that a target was vulnerable or that an attempt succeeded, and its timeline lists public proof-of-concept code from 2026-11-05 17:30 UTC (Previdian, 2026-11-07). The Hacker News, quoting a statement from Previdian's chief executive, reports that Previdian confirmed successful root access on a honeypot running Alpine Linux and OpenSSH, where the attacker used oversized passwords to bypass authentication and ran the reconnaissance commands id, uname and hostname in non-interactive SSH sessions, and that the first attempt came less than nine hours after the CVE was published (The Hacker News, 2026-11-06); the honeypot detail is not on Previdian's page, and the article's own total, eight attempts from one address geolocated to Japan, differs from the page's totals. Previdian's page lists the flaw as not in CISA's catalog (Previdian, 2026-11-07).

Alpine's advisory adds that updating the package does not restart a running sshd, so sshd must be restarted, and that on exposed machines the administrator should review doas use and recently created users, files and authorized keys, treating the machine as compromised if a login cannot be ruled out (Alpine Linux, 2026-11-05). No vendor or authority source reports attacks on production systems.
